name: Egg Bhurji
cuisine: Maharashtrian / Mumbai street food ("anda bhurji", served at roadside bhurji-pav carts and Irani cafés), also cooked at home across North and West India

ingredients.name: Groundnut oil (or any neutral cooking oil)
Onion (pyaz/kanda)
ingredients.householdMeasure: 1 small onion, finely chopped (about ½ cup)

ingredients.name: Tomato (tamatar)
ingredients.householdMeasure: 1 small tomato, finely chopped (about ⅓ cup)

ingredients.name: Capsicum (shimla mirch), green
ingredients.householdMeasure: 2 tbsp, finely chopped (optional, Mumbai cart style)

equipment: Kadai, tawa or 8-inch frying pan (non-stick is easiest for beginners; steel or iron works if you keep the heat at medium and keep stirring)
Mixing bowl for beating the eggs
Flat spatula (wooden or silicone is gentlest on non-stick)
Measuring spoons (normal teaspoons are a fine stand-in)
Optional for serving: a tawa to toast pav

steps.title: Chop the onion
steps.text: Peel and finely chop 60 g (1 small) onion.
steps.tip: Chop fine. Big onion pieces stay crunchy because the cook is short.
steps.visualCue: Small, even pieces about the size of a lentil.
steps.cameraCheck: About ½ cup chopped onion on the board
steps.videoShot: The knife rocking through the onion.
steps.watchOut: Big onion chunks stay crunchy because the cook is short; if you see pieces bigger than a fingernail, chop them again.

steps.title: Chop the tomato
steps.text: Finely chop 60 g (1 small) tomato.
steps.visualCue: Small, juicy cubes; no big skin pieces.
steps.cameraCheck: About ⅓ cup chopped tomato
steps.videoShot: The knife dicing the tomato.
steps.watchOut: A blunt knife squashes the tomato into a watery pulp on the board; use a sharp knife, or the masala will turn too wet later.

steps.title: Chop the capsicum (optional)
steps.text: Finely chop 20 g capsicum.
steps.visualCue: Tiny green squares
steps.cameraCheck: 2 tbsp chopped capsicum
steps.videoShot: Knife chopping capsicum strips into cubes.
steps.watchOut: Large capsicum strips stay hard in the short cook; keep the pieces about the size of a pea.

steps.title: Chop the chilli and coriander
steps.text: Finely chop 1 green chilli (5 g) and 1 tbsp (5 g) coriander leaves. Keep them in separate small heaps.
steps.tip: Remove the chilli seeds if you want less heat.
steps.visualCue: Fine green flecks, two heaps
steps.cameraCheck: The chilli and the coriander side by side
steps.videoShot: Coriander being chopped.
steps.watchOut: Touching your eyes after cutting chilli stings badly; wash your hands with soap before doing anything else.

steps.title: Crack the eggs
steps.text: Crack 3 eggs into the bowl, one at a time.
steps.tip: Crack each egg on a flat surface, not the bowl rim, to get fewer shell pieces.
steps.visualCue: Three whole yolks, no shell bits
steps.cameraCheck: 3 eggs in the bowl
steps.videoShot: An egg cracking on the rim of the bowl.
steps.watchOut: Shell pieces falling in; fish them out with a larger piece of shell, not a finger. Crack each egg into the bowl separately so one bad egg does not spoil the rest.

steps.title: Beat the eggs
steps.text: Add a pinch of the salt (about a third of it) and beat with a fork.
steps.visualCue: An even, pale-yellow mix with light froth and no streaks of white.
steps.cameraCheck: The beaten eggs in the bowl
steps.videoShot: The fork whisking in quick circles.
steps.watchOut: Streaks of clear white left in the mix cook into rubbery white lumps; keep beating until the colour is even.

steps.title: Heat the fat
steps.text: Put the pan on medium heat. Add 1 tsp (5 ml) oil and 1 tsp of the butter (keep ½ tsp butter for the end).
steps.visualCue: The butter melts and foams lightly; it does not brown.
steps.cameraCheck: The pan with melted butter and oil
steps.videoShot: Butter melting and swirling into the oil.
steps.watchOut: Brown butter and a burnt smell mean the heat is too high; lower the flame, and if it has darkened, wipe the pan and start again.

steps.title: Add the cumin (optional)
steps.text: Add ¼ tsp (1 g) cumin seeds.
steps.visualCue: The seeds sizzle and turn a shade darker.
steps.cameraCheck: Sizzling cumin in the pan
steps.videoShot: Cumin hitting the hot fat.
steps.watchOut: Cumin turns black and bitter in seconds; add the onion at once when it sizzles and darkens a shade.

steps.title: Sauté the onion
steps.text: Add the chopped onion and stir.
steps.visualCue: Soft and translucent, with light golden edges, not dark brown.
steps.cameraCheck: The onions in the pan
steps.videoShot: The spatula turning the onions.
steps.watchOut: Dark brown or crisp edges mean the heat is too high and will make the bhurji taste bitter; lower the flame and add 1 tsp water if the pan looks dry.

steps.title: Add the chilli and ginger-garlic paste
steps.text: Add the green chilli and 1 tsp (5 g) ginger-garlic paste. Stir.
steps.tip: If it starts to stick, add 1 tsp water and keep stirring.
steps.visualCue: The raw garlic smell fades and it smells cooked and sweet.
steps.cameraCheck: The paste mixed through the onion
steps.videoShot: The paste being stirred in.
steps.watchOut: The paste sticks and scorches at the bottom of the pan; stir constantly, and if it catches, add 1 tsp water.

steps.title: Add the capsicum (optional)
steps.text: Add the capsicum and stir.
steps.visualCue: The capsicum turns bright green and slightly soft.
steps.cameraCheck: Green flecks in the onion mix
steps.videoShot: Capsicum tossed through.
steps.watchOut: Capsicum cooked too long turns dull olive and watery; 1 minute is enough.

steps.title: Add the tomato and remaining salt
steps.text: Add the chopped tomato and the rest of the ¼ tsp salt. Stir.
steps.tip: Press the tomato pieces with the back of the spatula to speed this up.
steps.visualCue: The tomato breaks down into a soft, saucy mash.
steps.cameraCheck: The mashed tomato-onion masala
steps.videoShot: The spatula pressing the tomato.
steps.watchOut: A masala that is still wet when the eggs go in makes a soggy bhurji; cook until the tomato juices have mostly dried up and the oil shows at the edges.

steps.title: Lower the heat and add the spices
steps.text: Turn the flame to low. Add ⅛ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and ½ tsp pav bhaji masala. Stir.
steps.tip: Low heat stops the powders from burning and turning bitter.
steps.visualCue: The masala turns deep orange-red and the oil starts to show at the edges.
steps.cameraCheck: The red masala in the pan
steps.videoShot: The spices sprinkled on, then stirred.
steps.watchOut: Powdered spices burn within seconds on high heat and taste bitter; if they darken or smell acrid, add 1 tbsp water at once and carry on.

steps.title: Add the eggs
steps.text: Turn the flame back to medium-low. Pour in the beaten eggs.
steps.visualCue: The eggs spread over the masala and start to set at the edges.
steps.cameraCheck: Eggs poured over the masala
steps.videoShot: The yellow egg stream hitting the red masala.
steps.watchOut: High heat sets the eggs at once into tough, brown-edged curds; keep the flame at medium-low.

steps.title: Let the eggs set briefly
steps.text: Leave them untouched.
steps.visualCue: The bottom and edges look opaque and just set.
steps.cameraCheck: The edges setting in the pan
steps.videoShot: Close-up of the edges turning from glossy to matte.
steps.watchOut: Stirring too early gives a runny, mixed-up mush instead of soft curds; wait until the edges are set.

steps.title: Scramble the eggs
steps.text: Push the set parts from the edges to the middle and mix them with the masala, folding gently.
steps.tip: Take the pan off the heat when the eggs still look slightly wet. They keep cooking from the heat of the pan.
steps.visualCue: Soft, moist curds coated in masala; a little wet egg still visible.
steps.cameraCheck: The soft scramble in the pan
steps.videoShot: The spatula folding big, soft curds.
steps.watchOut: Dry, rubbery, pale-brown curds mean the eggs are overcooked; take the pan off the heat while they still look slightly wet, because they keep cooking in the hot pan.
steps.funFact: Bhurji is cooked until fairly dry, unlike the Parsi dish akuri, whose eggs are left softer and runnier (Wikipedia, Egg bhurji).

steps.title: Break into smaller pieces (Mumbai style)
steps.text: Chop through the curds a few times with the edge of the spatula.
steps.visualCue: Small, crumbly-but-moist pieces, like coarse crumbs.
steps.cameraCheck: The finely broken bhurji
steps.videoShot: The spatula edge chopping the eggs on the pan.
steps.watchOut: Over-chopping on the heat dries the bhurji out; keep it to a few quick cuts and then stop.

steps.title: Finish with butter and coriander
steps.text: Switch off the heat. Add the remaining ½ tsp butter and the chopped coriander. Fold once.
steps.visualCue: A buttery gloss and green flecks all through
steps.cameraCheck: Butter melting on the bhurji
steps.videoShot: The butter melting and coriander falling in.
steps.watchOut: Coriander stirred in on the flame wilts and turns dark; add it only after the heat is off.

steps.title: Taste and adjust
steps.text: Taste a little. Add a pinch more salt or a squeeze of lemon only if needed.
steps.visualCue: Balanced: salty, spicy, slightly tangy.
steps.cameraCheck: The finished bhurji in the pan
steps.videoShot: A spoon lifting a bite.
steps.watchOut: Too much salt cannot be taken out; add only a pinch at a time, since the butter and eggs already carry some salt. If it is too salty, serve with plain bread or roti.

steps.title: Plate it
steps.text: Spoon the bhurji onto a plate straight away.
steps.visualCue: Moist, orange-yellow crumbs with green flecks; no liquid pooling.
steps.cameraCheck: The served plate
steps.videoShot: A slow pan across the finished plate.
steps.watchOut: Leaving it in the hot pan keeps the eggs cooking and they turn dry within a minute or two; plate it at once.

reasons: three whole eggs give about 21 g of complete protein, and the dish is not deep-fried. The home version uses 1 tsp oil and 1½ tsp butter and adds about 140 g of onion, tomato and capsicum. Points come off for the saturated fat (about 9 g) and cholesterol (about 575 mg) from the yolks plus butter, and for about 850 mg sodium. Street versions often use a large dollop of butter or extra oil and more salt and masala, and are almost always eaten with 2–4 butter-toasted pav (refined flour). That can push a plate past 700 kcal.

researchRating.basis: egg bhurji is one of India's most-loved quick egg dishes and a Mumbai street-food classic. Recipe pages re-checked this run score very high (Indian Healthy Recipes 4.99/5 from 214 votes; Piping Pot Curry about 4.98/5 from about 38 votes; Plattershare 4.75/5 from 4; Cubes n Juliennes 4.60/5 from 5; Ministry of Curry 4.54/5 from 13 votes), and Mumbai food writers (Homegrown, Finely Chopped, Curly Tales) celebrate bhurji-pav carts and Irani cafés for it. Small deductions because it is seen as a simple everyday dish rather than a showpiece, and because many people find street versions too oily or buttery.

storage: Best eaten fresh. Leftovers can go in the fridge in an airtight box within 2 hours of cooking and keep for up to 2 days (cooked egg dishes are generally safe for 3–4 days, but texture suffers after day 1). Freezing is not recommended; the eggs turn watery and rubbery. To reheat, warm in a pan on low heat with 1 tsp water for 1–2 min, stirring, or microwave covered in 20-second bursts until steaming hot.
leftoverRemix: Bhurji cheese toastie. Spread leftover bhurji between two slices of bread with 1 tsp green chutney and a slice of cheese. Toast on a tawa with ½ tsp butter for about 2 min per side, pressing with a spatula, until golden and the cheese melts. Cut diagonally and serve with ketchup.
burnOff: about 5.2 km of running (366 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 7.3 km of brisk walking (about 1 hr 30 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.). With 2 buttered pav (about 605 kcal): about 8.6 km running or 12 km walking (est.).

navratri.reason: egg, onion and garlic are avoided in vrat (common rule set assumed)

ekadashi.reason: egg, onion and garlic are avoided (common rule set assumed; families differ)

jain.reason: contains egg, onion, garlic and ginger root

ramadan.reason: a protein-rich, quick sehri dish (about 21 g protein from 3 eggs, no halal-meat issue as eggs are not meat); sodium is about 850 mg (about 43% of the daily limit), so go easy on the salt and eat it with a phulka or whole-wheat toast rather than butter pav

jain.reason: egg is the main ingredient, and the recipe also has onion (60 g), ginger-garlic paste (5 g) and fresh chilli; no Jain version is appropriate (see Diet variants)

vegan.reason: 3 eggs and 7 g butter; the dish is defined by egg (see Diet variants)

pescatarian.reason: egg and dairy are allowed in a pescatarian diet and the recipe has no meat

sattvik.reason: drop the onion (60 g) and the ginger-garlic paste (5 g, use ginger paste only; see Sattvik variant). Note that sattvik rule sets also often avoid egg itself (common rule set assumed)

glutenFree.reason: no wheat, rava, maida or hing in the recipe; check the pav bhaji masala label for added wheat fillers, and note that the pav served alongside is wheat

dairyFree.reason: swap the 7 g butter for 7 ml more oil (see Dairy-free variant)

variants.reason: egg is the main ingredient (Jain rules exclude egg, and the recipe also has onion, garlic and ginger root); a Jain "bhurji" would be a paneer or besan dish, which is a different dish (see FitPlate's Paneer Bhurji, dish 69, which has a Jain version)
the dish is defined by egg; a tofu scramble is a different dish (FitPlate's Paneer Bhurji, dish 69, has a tofu bhurji vegan version)
main recipe already gluten-free (check the pav bhaji masala label; serve with rice, phulka made from jowar/bajra or gluten-free toast instead of pav)
